x.t: A spacecraft reaches Mercury after a trip of about eight years
b: A spacecraft called BepiColombo is now going around [[mercury|Mercury]]. Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun.
BepiColombo left Earth in 2018. Its trip took about eight years. On the way, it flew past planets nine times. A planet's [[gravity|pull]] helped it slow down or turn.
Europe and Japan made it together. In December, it will split into two. Science work is due to start in 2027.

o.t: BepiColombo spacecraft goes into orbit around Mercury
b: BepiColombo, a joint mission of the [[esa|European Space Agency]] (ESA) and Japan's space agency JAXA, went into [[orbit|orbit]] around [[mercury|Mercury]], the closest planet to the Sun, on Saturday 21 November. An orbit is a curved path around a planet. Firing its thrusters, small rocket engines, slowed it so Mercury's [[gravity|gravity]] could capture it.

It was launched in 2018 and travelled for about eight years, making nine flybys: Earth once, Venus twice and Mercury six times. A flyby uses a planet's gravity, the force pulling objects together, to slow a spacecraft or change its direction.

BepiColombo carries two spacecraft, ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mio, due to separate on 9 and 10 December 2026. MPO will map Mercury's surface and what it is made of. Mio will study Mercury's magnetic field, its area of magnetic force. Science work is due to start in April 2027.

stories.think: If you could send a spacecraft to any planet, which one would you choose, and what would you want to find out?

quiz.q: How many flybys did BepiColombo make on its way to Mercury?

x.t: India make the biggest Test score ever in New Zealand
b: India made the biggest Test score ever in New Zealand. A Test is a long cricket match. They scored 720 runs in Wellington.
Then India [[declare|declared]]. That means they chose to stop batting. Now they have time to get New Zealand out.
New Zealand have 119 runs, with two batters out. They are 233 runs behind. Monday is the last day.

o.t: India declare on a record 720 as New Zealand try to save Test
b: India declared on 720 for 9, meaning 720 runs with nine batters out, on Sunday 22 November. It was day four of the five-day first Test against New Zealand at the [[basin-reserve|Basin Reserve]] in Wellington. It is the highest Test total ever in New Zealand. To [[declare|declare]] is to choose to stop batting, leaving time to bowl the other side out.

New Zealand made 368 in their first [[innings|innings]], a team's turn to bat, so India led by 352. KL Rahul scored 136 and Rishabh Pant 128, his ninth Test [[century|century]], a score of 100 runs or more.

At the end of the day, New Zealand were 119 for 2, still 233 behind, with Devon Conway on 59 and still batting. On Monday, the last day, India will try to get eight more batters out, while New Zealand will try to bat all day to save the match.

stories.think: On Monday, New Zealand will try to bat all day to save the match. Is it harder to score lots of runs, or to stay in and not get out? Why?

quiz.q: What score did India declare on?

x.t: Some countries say no to a new climate plan
b: Countries met in Antalya, Turkey, to talk about the climate. The talks went on for two extra days.
Early on Sunday, a new [[draft|draft]] plan came out. It did not name [[fossil-fuel|fossil fuels]] like oil and gas. Some countries said the plan did not do enough.
Nearly every country has to agree to a plan. By Sunday afternoon, they had not all agreed.

o.t: No agreement on new COP31 climate draft as some countries object
b: The [[cop31|COP31]] United Nations climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, were due to end on Friday 20 November but ran for two extra days. Early on Sunday, a new [[draft|draft]], or early version of the deal, was released.

The draft did not name [[fossil-fuel|fossil fuels]], such as coal, oil and gas. It referred instead to an earlier COP agreement to move away from them. The [[european-union|European Union]] and Panama said they could not support it. Countries disagreed about whether the deal should name fossil fuels.

A deal needs [[consensus|consensus]], which means broad agreement among the nearly 200 countries taking part. By Sunday afternoon in Turkey, the countries had not all agreed on the plan. The next talks, COP32, are planned for Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, in November 2027.

stories.think: Why do you think it can be hard for nearly 200 countries to agree on one plan?

quiz.q: How many countries took part in the COP31 talks?

x.t: Verstappen wins a close night race in Las Vegas
b: Max Verstappen won the Las Vegas Grand Prix. It is a Formula 1 car race held at night. He started in [[pole-position|pole position]], right at the front.
The race was 50 [[lap|laps]] of the track. The lead changed 35 times. Lando Norris came second, less than one second behind.
Oscar Piastri started in 17th place. He passed many cars and finished third. Verstappen is second in this year's points table.

o.t: Verstappen wins Las Vegas Grand Prix after 35 lead changes
b: [[max-verstappen|Max Verstappen]] of the Red Bull team won the Las Vegas Grand Prix, a Formula 1 race held at night in the United States. It was run on Saturday 21 November, which was Sunday morning in India. Verstappen started from [[pole-position|pole position]], the front place on the starting grid, and it was his third win in Las Vegas.

The race lasted 50 [[lap|laps]], or trips around the track, and the lead changed 35 times. Lando Norris of McLaren finished second, just 0.639 seconds behind. His teammate Oscar Piastri was third after starting 17th. Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes came fourth.

Starting first gives a driver a head start, but a race is won over many laps. Antonelli was already sure to finish first this season, so he is this year's [[champion|champion]]. Verstappen is second in the standings, the table of points each driver has scored this season.

stories.think: The Las Vegas race is held at night. What might be different for drivers racing at night?

quiz.q: Where did Oscar Piastri start the race?

x.t: Fewer seals would barely help salmon, a study finds
b: Seals, sea lions and seabirds eat salmon. Would having fewer of them help salmon? Scientists tested this on a computer.
Having fewer of these animals barely helped salmon. Why? These [[predator|hunters]] also eat other fish. Some of those fish eat young salmon.
Everything in the ocean is linked in a [[food-web|food web]]. Changing one part changes others. In the computer test, fewer hake fish helped salmon more.

o.t: Removing seals and sea lions would barely help salmon, study finds
b: A study published in the [[journal|journal]] Science on 19 November found that removing seals, sea lions and seabirds across a wide area off the US West Coast would bring little or no benefit to Chinook and coho, two kinds of salmon. Lead author Dylan Gomes worked at NOAA, a US science agency, and Oregon State University.

The team used an [[ecosystem|ecosystem]] model, a computer program copying how living things in an area affect each other. These [[predator|predators]], animals that hunt others, also eat Pacific hake and other fish that eat young salmon or compete with them for food. The hake there weigh about 370 times as much as all the seals and sea lions together.

In the model, reducing hake helped salmon more than reducing seals. The study did not test single spots on salmon routes, such as fish ladders, and the authors do not rule out removing particular animals there.

stories.think: Can you think of another way that changing one thing in nature could affect something else?

quiz.q: What did the scientists use to test their idea?

where.n: Ocean off the US West Coast

x.t: Lakshya Sen's 13-match winning run ends in Hong Kong
b: Lakshya Sen is a badminton player from India. He had won 13 matches in a row. That run ended on Saturday.
Anders Antonsen from Denmark beat him in the [[semi-final|semi-final]] of the Hong Kong Open. A semi-final decides who plays in the last match.
Sen won two [[tournament|tournaments]] earlier this month. Winning 13 in a row is hard to do. Antonsen's win took him into the [[final|final]].

o.t: Antonsen ends Lakshya Sen's 13-match run in Hong Kong semi-final
b: India's Lakshya Sen lost to Anders Antonsen of Denmark in the men's singles [[semi-final|semi-final]] of the Hong Kong Open badminton [[tournament|tournament]] on Saturday 21 November. A semi-final is one of two matches that decide who plays in the [[final|final]]. Antonsen won 21-13, 21-13, taking both games.

The defeat ended Sen's run of 13 wins in a row. Earlier in November he won two other tournaments, the Hylo Open and the Kumamoto Masters. Winning so many matches in a row is a big achievement, and even the best players lose sometimes.

India's men's [[doubles|doubles]] pair, Satwik Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty, also lost their semi-final. Doubles is a match with two players on each side. Antonsen's win sent him through to the final.

stories.think: Lakshya Sen won 13 matches in a row before he lost. What can a player learn from a loss after a long winning run?

quiz.q: Who beat Lakshya Sen in the Hong Kong Open semi-final?

bigStory.t: How far is one light-day from home?
bigStory.sub: Voyager 1, launched in 1977, reached one light-day from Earth on Wednesday

x.why: A spacecraft that left Earth in 1977 is still travelling. This week it got so far away that light needs a whole day to reach it.

o.why: A spacecraft launched in 1977 is still travelling, and its team on Earth still talks to it. This week it reached a distance so great that a radio signal, moving at the speed of light, needs 24 hours to get there.

facts: about one light-day: how far light travels in 24 hours
how long a radio signal from Earth now takes to reach it
the day it reached one light-day

days.o: NASA launched Voyager 1 on 5 September 1977. It flew past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, and in 1990 it took a picture of Earth known as the Pale Blue Dot. In 2012 it entered interstellar space, the space between the stars. It is run from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California.
days.x: Voyager 1 is a spacecraft. It left Earth in 1977. It flew past the planets Jupiter and Saturn. In 1990 it took a picture of Earth from very far away.

days.o: A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, about 25.9 billion kilometres. Light reaches the Moon in about 1.3 seconds, and sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. After sunset today, Tuesday 17 November, NASA invites people to flash VGR, Voyager's three-letter call sign, in Morse code towards the sky with a torch.
days.x: A light-day is how far light travels in one day. Sunlight reaches us in about 8 minutes. After sunset today, people can flash a torch for Voyager. Ask a grown-up to help.

days.o: NASA worked out that Voyager 1 would reach one light-day from Earth on Wednesday 18 November. No spacecraft has travelled this far before. A radio signal now takes about 24 hours to reach it, and its reply takes another day to come back. Voyager 2 is expected to reach one light-day in 2035.
days.x: On Wednesday, Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth. No spacecraft has gone this far before. A message now takes about a day to get there.

days.o: NASA talks to Voyager 1 by radio through its Deep Space Network, a set of giant radio antennas at three sites: Goldstone in California, near Madrid in Spain and near Canberra in Australia. The sites are placed around the world so that they can keep in contact with a spacecraft as Earth turns. Each site has one antenna that is 70 metres across. A radio signal now takes about 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and its reply takes another 24 hours to come back, so a message and its answer make a two-day round trip.
days.x: NASA talks to Voyager 1 with radio signals. It uses giant radio antennas in California, Spain and Australia. A message takes about a day to reach Voyager 1. The reply takes another day to come back.

days.o: On Wednesday 18 November Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth. Its power source makes about 4 watts less every year, so NASA has been switching off instruments to save power. Even after it falls silent, it will keep travelling. It will take about 300 years to reach the inner edge of a distant region called the Oort Cloud. In about 40,000 years it is expected to pass another star. It carries a Golden Record with sounds, music and images from Earth, and greetings in 55 languages. On 14 November, NASA found that Voyager 1's signal was reaching Earth without its usual science data. NASA thinks the problem is likely to be in the onboard computer that collects the data, and engineers are working on it.
days.x: On Wednesday, Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth. Its power gets a little weaker every year. Even when it falls silent, it will keep travelling. It carries a Golden Record with sounds, music and pictures from Earth. As of 19 November, Voyager 1's messages were arriving without their science data. Engineers are working on the problem.

x.t: How a spacecraft goes into orbit
b: An orbit is a path that one object in space takes around another.
If a spacecraft reaches a planet too fast, it speeds past the planet. So it has to slow down.
Then the planet's pull, called gravity, can catch it. The BepiColombo spacecraft was due to go into orbit around Mercury on 21 November.
x.remember: A spacecraft flying to a planet has to slow down. Then the planet's pull, called gravity, can catch it.
x.q: What must a spacecraft do so a planet's gravity can catch it?

o.t: How does a spacecraft go into orbit around a planet?
b: An orbit is a regular, repeating path that one object in space takes around another. The BepiColombo spacecraft was due to enter orbit around the planet Mercury on 21 November.

An orbit is a balance between two things. One is the spacecraft's momentum, which is its tendency to keep moving in a straight line. The other is the pull of the planet's gravity. If the momentum is too great, the spacecraft speeds past the planet. So it has to slow down so the planet's gravity can catch it. When the two are balanced, the spacecraft is always falling towards the planet but never hits it.

Mercury is hard to reach because it is so close to the Sun. The Sun's gravity pulls a spacecraft towards it, so it has to keep braking on the way. To help it slow down, BepiColombo flew close past planets nine times.
o.remember: An orbit is a balance between a spacecraft's momentum and a planet's gravity. A spacecraft must arrive slowly enough for the planet's gravity to catch it.
o.q: What happens if a spacecraft's momentum is too great when it reaches a planet?
